sentences.pattern: Although + an AI system + can identify patterns in data, it cannot make + an ethical or professional judgement + without human input.
sentences.cn: 尽管某人工智能系统能够识别某种规律，但没有人工参与，它无法决定价值判断。
sentences.example: Although an AI system can identify patients at higher statistical risk, it cannot determine how limited treatment should be allocated without human input.

sentences.pattern: The more serious the consequences of + an automated decision + are, the stronger + human oversight + should be.
sentences.cn: 自动化决定的影响越重大，监督或保障措施就应越严格。
sentences.example: The more consequential an automated hiring decision is, the stronger the opportunity for human review should be.

sentences.pattern: Rather than asking whether AI can + perform a task, institutions should ask whether it can do so + accurately and fairly.
sentences.cn: 与其问人工智能能否完成某项任务，机构更应问它在什么条件下能够达到某项标准。
sentences.example: Rather than asking whether AI can mark essays, schools should ask under what conditions it can do so consistently and fairly.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: AI should augment professional expertise in high-stakes fields.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: In medicine and law, artificial intelligence is most valuable when it extends rather than replaces expert judgement.
writingIdeas.argument: An algorithm can scan more records than one professional and draw attention to patterns that might otherwise be missed. However, an unusual patient or legal case may fall outside the examples on which the system was trained. A qualified professional can interpret context, explain uncertainty and accept responsibility for the final choice. Combining computational speed with accountable judgement therefore offers a safer advantage than allowing either component to operate alone.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Public bodies must test unequal effects before deployment.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: An automated system that performs well on average may still disadvantage a particular group.
writingIdeas.argument: Suppose a voice-recognition service is highly accurate for the speakers most common in its dataset but frequently misunderstands a regional accent. If access to benefits depends on that service, average accuracy conceals a serious barrier. Agencies should test results separately across relevant populations and offer an accessible human alternative. Where a consistent gap cannot be corrected, efficiency is not a sufficient reason to keep the system in use.

speaking.question: Describe an AI-based tool that you have found useful.
speaking.answer: I use a transcription tool after online meetings. It produces a rough written record, separates speakers and lets me search for a particular decision instead of replaying an hour of audio. The main benefit is not perfect accuracy but speed. Names and technical terms are sometimes wrong, so I compare important sections with the recording before sharing the notes. I also tell participants that transcription is being used because conversations can contain sensitive information. The tool has reduced a repetitive task, while the responsibility for checking and summarising still belongs to me. That balance is why I find it genuinely useful rather than simply impressive.

speaking.question: Which decisions should never be left entirely to artificial intelligence?
speaking.answer: Decisions involving basic rights, severe punishment or life-changing medical treatment should always include accountable human judgement. AI may organise evidence or estimate risk, but statistics cannot settle questions about compassion, acceptable uncertainty or competing public values. People also need a meaningful explanation and a route of appeal. Human involvement is not automatically fair, of course, so reviewers need evidence and clear standards too. The essential point is that an institution cannot avoid responsibility by saying a system made the decision.

reading.title: The Quiet Work of Labelling Data
paragraphs: Public discussion of artificial intelligence often concentrates on powerful models and specialist engineers. Less visible is the human labour used to prepare examples from which many systems learn. Workers label road signs in photographs, judge whether comments are offensive or outline organs in medical scans. Their decisions convert complicated reality into categories a computer can process.

The task can appear straightforward until cases become uncertain. Is a partly hidden bicycle still a bicycle? Does a sarcastic sentence express hostility, humour or both? Project instructions, usually written before every ambiguity is known, may not provide an answer. Labelers then rely on experience or make inconsistent choices, which later appear to the model as if they were objective facts. A dataset of millions of examples can therefore contain the accumulated interpretation of workers whose names never accompany it.

Working conditions influence quality. Tight deadlines reward speed, while payment per item may discourage careful consultation. Some content-moderation datasets also expose workers to disturbing material. Companies have improved guidance and wellbeing support in certain projects, yet long subcontracting chains can make responsibility difficult to locate. The organisation deploying a system may know little about the people who produced its training categories.

Researchers increasingly measure disagreement instead of forcing every item into one accepted label. If several careful reviewers interpret a sentence differently, that variation can be useful evidence about the sentence rather than mere noise to remove. Models designed to express uncertainty may preserve such information, whereas a single-label dataset hides it. This approach requires more time and complicates performance scores, which helps explain why it is not universal.

Data labelling is neither an insignificant preliminary step nor a guarantee of intelligence. It is a sequence of human judgements, made under particular instructions and economic conditions, that shapes what a system can recognise. Evaluating AI responsibly consequently involves looking behind the final interface—not only at code and accuracy figures, but also at whose interpretations became data and whose uncertainty disappeared.
